source.title: Harmless Interpolation of Noisy Data in Regression
source.authors: Vidya K. Muthukumar; Kailas Vodrahalli; Vignesh Subramanian; Anant Sahai

record.tranche_reason: The study tests interpolation risk as feature count grows in linear regression and refines the scope of double descent: it reports a clear example, but also emphasizes dependence on feature structure and signal representation.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own test-MSE results for feature-count sweeps in linear regression. Results cited from other work, including double descent in deep networks and ridge comparisons, are not recorded as rows. The noise-variance curves in Figure 7 are not described condition by condition in the text.
record.test_reason: In overparameterized linear regression the study reports its own test-MSE sweeps over feature count. These show a spike at d=n and then a decay for some feature families and estimators, but not for others. It also argues that the second descent beats the first only when the model is misspecified. That bears on V4 outside deep networks. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that interpolating noise becomes harmless only with heavy overparameterization: ideal MSE scales as σ²n/d. The min-ℓ2 interpolator bleeds signal unless a strong prior favours the true features, and parsimonious interpolators (OMP, BP) fit noise harmfully. Hybrid two-step interpolators are order-optimal, yet interpolation is practically always worse than regularization. A second descent beating the first requires model misspecification. Implications for deep networks remain unclear.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and evaluates interpolating estimators in overparameterized linear regression, rather than scaling deep neural network model size. It includes theoretical bounds and feature-count sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature family and feature weighting affect the behavior; the text contrasts Gaussian and Legendre features with Vandermonde features, and discusses dependence on signal representation and sampling regularity.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Information Theory
record.problems: The empirical examples are synthetic linear-regression settings rather than deep networks. The clear Figure 3 example uses n=10. Several figure values are not stated numerically in the text, and some conditions are described only through plots. The ideal interpolator requires knowledge of the true signal and is presented as a fundamental benchmark, not a practical estimator.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 7's separate noise-variance curves are not included because the text does not report their condition-specific outcomes; the plotted values alone do not support a textual verdict on noise dependence. Figure 9's confidence-interval comparisons are also omitted because the text discusses changes in sampling regularity and variability near the threshold but does not give a complete curve-by-curve double-descent result for each method.

untested.parts: Sample-wise non-monotonicity at a fixed model size.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Peak dependence on noise level: the Figure 7 σ² sweep is not described per condition. Multiple descent and disappearance under optimal ridge are only cited from [6] and argued, not measured.
Re-plotting against an effective parameter count. The survival and contamination factors relate to effective ranks but are not used to recount complexity.
Non-linear model classes (kernels, trees, networks); classification losses.

missing.what: Min-ℓ2 interpolator on Example 4 (sparse signal, whitened Gaussian): test MSE converges to the zero-fit null risk as d grows, i.e. poor generalization past the threshold. OMP, BP and hybrid interpolators are also on the same plot.
Analytic argument that in correctly specified models the second descent cannot beat the first; only approximation benefit from misspecification allows it.
Converse-bound curves for Legendre and Fourier (regular and random) and Gaussian features at n=15, with a peak and variability at the threshold and convergence for d/n≥10.
Regular vs random training points change the size and variability of the peak at d≈n for ideal, min-ℓ2 and hybrid interpolators.

record.verdict_notes: The 'labels' entry for Example 4 rests on text and needs a new row. The text is internally inconsistent on Example 5: it first says improved approximability is 'not the main reason', then calls it 'the primary explanation' of double descent. Most evidence is figure-only, with no numbers in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and the model-size curve in deep networks.
Increasing sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The claim's breadth across model classes generally; the study evaluates linear-regression feature families and interpolators.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs and samples.

Whether label noise drives the peak, multiple or triple descent, and disappearance of the peak under optimally tuned regularization. Figure 7 varies noise variance, but the text does not describe the variance-specific curve outcomes.
Recounting complexity by effective parameters to turn the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Unwhitened Vandermonde polynomial features, min-ℓ2 interpolator
source_check.reason: Section 3 explicitly states that the spike-and-decay properties do not manifest for Vandermonde features. R3 supports this verdict after correcting its subject.

relationships.condition: Parsimonious interpolators (OMP to completion, basis pursuit) fitting pure noise
relationships.reason: Past the threshold, test MSE falls only slightly and negligibly, logarithmically per Theorem 2, so there is little second descent (R5–R12).
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE improved only negligibly beyond interpolation in fixed-sample sweeps of OMP and basis pursuit.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Parsimonious interpolators (OMP to completion, basis pursuit) fitting pure noise
source_check.reason: For the fixed-n sweeps R5–R8, Section 5.1 calls the improvement negligible relative to ideal interpolation, which the rules classify as absent. R9–R12 jointly vary n and d and cannot independently test V4. Theorem 2 supplies lower bounds, not a universal logarithmic decay law.

relationships.condition: Whitened iid Gaussian features, k=500-sparse signal, n=5000, min-ℓ2 interpolator (Example 4, Fig. 7)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows: test MSE converges to the null risk of predicting zero because of signal bleed. The authors also argue a second descent beating the first requires misspecification.
relationships.display_finding: The minimum-ℓ2 interpolator's test MSE converged to the zero predictor's risk because of signal bleed, while beating the first minimum required misspecification.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Whitened iid Gaussian features, k=500-sparse signal, n=5000, min-ℓ2 interpolator (Example 4, Fig. 7)
source_check.reason: Convergence to null risk establishes poor signal recovery, but does not establish absence of post-threshold risk improvement. V4 does not require beating the first minimum or the zero predictor. Section 6.1 discusses the stronger requirement of a second descent better than the first.
